text: Everything so far in this chapter has been an operational defense — limit queries, watch for patterns, minimize output. Differential privacy is different in kind. It's a mathematical guarantee bounding exactly how much the presence or absence of any single record in a dataset can change the output of a computation performed on it, and it closes this chapter by going after the root of the problem instead of the symptoms.

That guarantee is tuned by a parameter called epsilon, the privacy budget. Smaller epsilon means more statistical noise and a stronger guarantee; larger epsilon means less noise and a weaker one. This is a real tradeoff dial, not a toggle — more privacy costs some accuracy, because the same noise that provides the guarantee also blurs the signal. And because bounding any single record's influence removes the confidence gap membership inference depends on, choosing epsilon deliberately is what actually defeats that attack from Lesson 14, not just mitigates it.

The noise itself is calibrated to the sensitivity of the computation — how much a single record could possibly change the raw answer — so it masks exactly that worst case and no more. The Laplace mechanism is the simplest version: take the true answer, add noise scaled to sensitivity divided by epsilon, and a smaller epsilon produces a larger noise scale and a stronger guarantee.

Abadi and colleagues' 2016 paper pushed this guarantee back into the training process itself, with DP-SGD. It clips each training example's gradient contribution to a bounded maximum, so no single unusual record can dominate a step, then adds calibrated noise to the aggregated gradient before updating the model's weights. Tracked carefully across every training step, that produces a model with a provable privacy guarantee baked into its parameters.

This isn't confined to research papers. The U.S. Census Bureau adopted differential privacy for the 2020 Census to protect individual households while still publishing useful population statistics, and Apple and Google have both used differentially private mechanisms to collect telemetry without tying any single report back to a person.

That's the throughline for this whole chapter: extraction, inversion, and membership inference all exploit what a model is willing to reveal, and the real defenses run from rate limits and output minimization all the way down to a mathematical guarantee you can actually prove. Chapter 5 picks up a related but different question — not what a model reveals about its training data, but how it can be fooled, one input at a time.
